---
title: "Session 5: Many variables at once: PCA, heatmaps and PLS-DA"
engine: knitr
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
set.seed(2026)   # same jittered points at every render
library(mixOmics)
library(tidyverse)
library(pheatmap)
library(ggrepel)
metabolites <- read_csv("data/05/soybean_metabolites.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
root_wide <- metabolites %>%
  filter(organ == "root") %>%
  mutate(log_conc = log10(concentration)) %>%
  select(sample, genotype, water, heat, metabolite, log_conc) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = metabolite, values_from = log_conc)
root_matrix <- root_wide %>% select(-sample, -genotype, -water, -heat) %>% as.matrix()
rownames(root_matrix) <- root_wide$sample
root_pca <- prcomp(root_matrix, scale. = TRUE)
variance <- round(100 * summary(root_pca)$importance[2, ], 1)
```

## Biological question

Drought and the heatwave reduced the plants' biomass (Session 4). Do they also change
the plants' chemistry, the same way in the root, the leaf, and in what the roots release
into the soil?
:::

In Session 4, you analysed **one** variable at a time: the biomass, then the Shannon
diversity. Today, each sample comes with **dozens, then thousands of variables at
once**: the concentrations of 15 to 37 small molecules (metabolites) measured in the
root, the stem, the leaf and the root exudates of the same soybean plants, then 2,500
untargeted signals from the exudates. One boxplot per molecule would give you dozens of
plots and no overview. You will learn the classic tools to see the whole
table at once:

- **PCA** and **heatmaps with clustering**, which look for structure **without** being
  told which sample is which (unsupervised);
- **PLS-DA**, which **is** told the groups and looks for what separates them
  (supervised), and the trap that comes with it;
- the **volcano plot**: one test per molecule, as in Session 4, and why you must
  correct the p-values when you run many tests.

### Learning outcomes

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

- explain why concentrations are log-transformed and scaled before a multivariate
  analysis;
- turn a long table into a sample × variable matrix with `pivot_wider()`;
- run a PCA, read the share of variance of each axis, the scores (samples) and the
  loadings (variables);
- draw a heatmap with clustering, and read its trees;
- run a PLS-DA, and explain why a supervised method must always be cross-validated;
- run one test per variable, correct the p-values for multiple testing, and draw a
  volcano plot;
- say which method answers which question.

## Theory (≈45 min)

### 1. From one variable to many

Each sample now has one value per metabolite. For the analyses of today, the table must
have **one row per sample and one column per metabolite**: a **matrix**. Your data file
is long (one row per sample *and* metabolite, as in Session 4), so the first step is
`pivot_wider()`, the reverse of the `pivot_longer()` you used in Session 4.

Two more steps before any multivariate method:

- **log-transform**: concentrations go from 0.02 to about 190,000. On the raw scale, a few very
  abundant molecules would dominate everything. `log10()` turns ratios into differences:
  a molecule that doubles moves by the same amount, whether it is rare or abundant.
- **scale**: each metabolite is centred and divided by its standard deviation, so that
  each one has the same weight in the analysis (`scale. = TRUE` in `prcomp()`).

### 2. Unsupervised: PCA and clustering

A **PCA** (principal component analysis) summarises the 34 columns into a few new axes,
the **principal components**. PC1 is the direction along which the samples differ the
most, PC2 the next one, at right angles, and so on. Three things to read:

- the **share of variance** of each axis: how much of the differences between samples
  it captures;
- the **scores**: where each sample falls on the axes (the usual PCA plot);
- the **loadings**: how much each metabolite contributes to each axis, and in which
  direction.

A **heatmap with clustering** shows the whole matrix as colours, and reorders rows and
columns so that similar ones sit next to each other. The trees (dendrograms) show the
groups found.

In the practical, you first run a PCA on data you know without any biology: 41 decathlon
performances, 10 events each. You will see the axes rediscover the best athletes, and why
scaling matters when the variables are in different units (seconds and metres).

Both are **unsupervised**: they never see your labels (`water`, `heat`). If the samples
still group by condition, the condition is a major source of variation in the data.

### 3. Supervised: PLS-DA, and why it must be validated

A **PLS-DA** (partial least squares discriminant analysis) is told the groups, and looks
for the combination of metabolites that **best separates** them. It is useful to find
which molecules distinguish two conditions, but it is dangerous: with many variables
and few samples, it can separate **any** groups, even groups drawn at random. A
separation on the data the model learned from proves nothing.

The answer is **cross-validation**: hide part of the samples, train the model on the
rest, predict the hidden samples, repeat. Only the accuracy on samples the model did not
see tells you whether the separation is real. You will see this trap with your own eyes
in block D.

### 4. Many tests at once: the volcano plot

You can also test each metabolite on its own: one t-test per molecule, as in Session 4.
With 34 tests at the 5% level, you expect about 1 or 2 "significant" results **by chance
alone**. Correcting the p-values (here with the Benjamini-Hochberg method, which controls
the **false discovery rate**) keeps that under control.

A **volcano plot** shows all the tests at once: the effect on the x axis (log2 fold
change: positive means higher under drought), the evidence on the y axis
(−log10 of the adjusted p-value: the higher, the stronger).

**Which method, when?**

| Your question | Method | In R | Supervised? |
|---|---|---|---|
| What are the main patterns in the samples? Do they group by condition? | PCA | `prcomp()` | no |
| Which samples and which variables look alike? | heatmap with clustering | `pheatmap()` | no |
| Which combination of variables separates known groups? | PLS-DA, **always with cross-validation** | `plsda()`, `perf()` | yes |
| Which variables change between two groups, one by one? | one test per variable + FDR, volcano plot | `t.test()`, `p.adjust()` | (it is a test) |

### 5. Worked example: the metabolome of the soybean plants

Today's data come from the plants you met in Session 4, measured with two kinds of
metabolomics:

| | Targeted | Untargeted |
|---|---|---|
| What is measured | a chosen list of known molecules | every signal the machine detects |
| Each variable is | a named molecule, quantified | a "feature": a peak with a retention time and a mass (m/z) |
| How many variables today | 15 to 37 per organ | 2,500 in the exudates |
| Identity | known for sure | unknown for many; a **putative** name from a database search, with a confidence score |
| Good for | testing precise hypotheses, comparing known pathways | discovering what you did not think of looking for |

- **Root, stem, leaf** (targeted): the `omics_and_soil` plants, frozen at harvest and
  ground; 4 samples per cultivar and condition, each a pool of two plants.
- **Exudates** (targeted **and** untargeted): what the roots of the `exudates` plants
  released into a solution, collected at harvest; one sample per plant.

The exudates are the molecules the root gives to the soil: the food and the signals of
the bacteria you studied in Session 4.

## Your R toolbox

New tools today, on top of the Session 4 toolbox (still valid: see the
[Session 4 R toolbox](04_biological_tables_and_visualisation.qmd#your-r-toolbox)).

::: panel-tabset
## tidyr: long → wide

`pivot_wider()` is the reverse of `pivot_longer()`: it spreads one column into many.

```r
root_wide <- root_long %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = metabolite, values_from = log_conc)
```

- `names_from`: the column whose values become the **new column names** (here: the
  metabolite names);
- `values_from`: the column that fills the new columns (here: the log concentrations).

Then `select(-sample, ...)` and `as.matrix()` keep the numbers only, as a matrix, and
`rownames()` puts the sample names back on the rows.

**Common mistake.** Keeping a column that differs inside a sample (such as the raw
`concentration` next to `log_conc`): `pivot_wider()` then cannot put one sample on one
row. Select only the columns you need before pivoting.

## PCA (base R)

`prcomp()` is part of R itself: no package needed.

| Code | What it gives |
|---|---|
| `prcomp(matrix, scale. = TRUE)` | the PCA, each variable scaled |
| `summary(pca)$importance[2, ]` | the share of variance of each axis |
| `pca$x` | the **scores**: one row per sample, one column per axis |
| `pca$rotation` | the **loadings**: one row per variable, one column per axis |

**Reading the loadings.** A metabolite with a large negative loading on PC1 is high in
the samples on the left of the PCA plot; a large positive loading, high on the right.

**Common mistake.** Forgetting `scale. = TRUE`: the variables with the largest numbers
then decide everything.

## pheatmap

```r
pheatmap(t(root_matrix), scale = "row", annotation_col = annotation,
         show_colnames = FALSE, fontsize_row = 7)
```

- `t()` turns the matrix around: metabolites in rows, samples in columns;
- `scale = "row"`: each metabolite is shown as "above or below its own average"
  (z-score), otherwise the most abundant ones would fill the colour scale;
- `annotation_col`: a small table, one row per sample (with the sample names as row
  names), whose columns become coloured bars on top;
- the trees on the left and on top are the **clustering**: they are computed from the
  data, not from the annotation.

## mixOmics

The reference package for PLS-DA (and much more) in biology.

| Code | What it does |
|---|---|
| `plsda(matrix, groups, ncomp = 2)` | fits a PLS-DA with 2 components |
| `plotIndiv(model, ellipse = TRUE, legend = TRUE)` | the sample plot, with one ellipse per group |
| `predict(model, matrix)$class$max.dist` | the predicted group of each sample |
| `perf(model, validation = "Mfold", folds = 4, nrepeat = 10)` | cross-validation: 4 folds, repeated 10 times |
| `perf(...)$error.rate$BER` | the balanced error rate, per component (accuracy = 1 − error) |

**Install once, load every time.** `BiocManager::install("mixOmics", update = FALSE)`
runs once, in the Console (block A0). `library(mixOmics)` goes at the top of every
report. Never put an install line in your workbook: every Render would install it again.

**Common mistake: load it first.** mixOmics loads another package (MASS) that also has a
function called `select()`. Whatever is loaded **last** wins. So load `mixOmics`
**before** the tidyverse; otherwise `select()` stops working, with a confusing error
("unused argument").

**Documentation.** [mixomics.org](https://mixomics.org/)

## ggrepel

`geom_text_repel()` writes text labels on a plot and moves them so that they do not
overlap, unlike `geom_text()`.

```r
geom_text_repel(data = slice_min(root_tests, p_adjusted, n = 10),
                aes(label = metabolite), size = 3)
```

`data = ...` labels only some of the points: here, the 10 with the smallest adjusted
p-values (`slice_min()`, from dplyr).
:::

**B2. The drought hormone.** Abscisic acid (ABA) makes the leaves close their stomata, the
small pores through which they lose water. Look at it in the three organs (it is not on
the exudate list):

```r
aba <- metabolites %>%
  filter(metabolite == "Abscisic Acid")

ggplot(aba, aes(x = water, y = concentration, colour = heat)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ organ, scales = "free_y")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-b2
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Checkpoint B2: abscisic acid in the three organs."
aba <- metabolites %>% filter(metabolite == "Abscisic Acid")
ggplot(aba, aes(x = water, y = concentration, colour = heat)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ organ, scales = "free_y")
```

`scales = "free_y"` gives each organ its own y axis: the levels are very different
between organs. The workbook also computes the mean per organ and water regime, as in
Session 4.

**B3. Proline**, a small amino acid that protects cells when water is short. Same plot,
with one `___` to fill. It was only measured in the leaf and the stem.

```r
ggplot(metabolites, aes(x = log10(concentration))) +
```

### 15:35-15:45: Short break

### Warm-up: what a PCA does, on athletes (15:45-16:00, pairs)

Before 34 metabolites, a PCA on data you can check with common sense: 41 decathlon
performances (Decastar meeting and Athens Olympic Games, 2004; data of the FactoMineR
package). Each athlete did 10 events: four runs (times in seconds, small is good) and six
jumps and throws (metres, large is good).

**W1. The table.**

```r
decathlon <- read_csv("data/decathlon.csv")
glimpse(decathlon)
decathlon %>% count(competition)
```

**W2. Without and with scaling.** The same PCA twice: first with each event in its own
unit, then with every event scaled.

```r
events <- decathlon %>%
  select(run_100m:run_1500m) %>%
  as.matrix()
rownames(events) <- decathlon$athlete

decathlon %>% summarise(across(run_100m:run_1500m, sd))

pca_raw <- prcomp(events, scale. = FALSE)
round(pca_raw$rotation[, 1], 2)

decathlon_pca <- prcomp(events, scale. = TRUE)
decathlon_variance <- round(100 * summary(decathlon_pca)$importance[2, ], 1)
decathlon_variance
```

`across(run_100m:run_1500m, sd)` applies `sd()` to every column from `run_100m` to
`run_1500m`.

**W3. Arrows and points.** The **loadings** become arrows (one per event), the
**scores** points (one per athlete):

```r
decathlon_loadings <- as_tibble(decathlon_pca$rotation[, 1:2], rownames = "event")

ggplot(decathlon_loadings) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = event)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", decathlon_variance[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", decathlon_variance[2], "%)"))

decathlon_scores <- as_tibble(decathlon_pca$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  bind_cols(select(decathlon, athlete, competition, points))

ggplot(decathlon_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = points)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = athlete), size = 3) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", decathlon_variance[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", decathlon_variance[2], "%)"))

cor(decathlon_scores$PC1, decathlon_scores$points)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-w3
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Checkpoint W3: the loadings of the decathlon PCA, one arrow per event."
decathlon <- read_csv("data/05/decathlon.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
events <- decathlon %>% select(run_100m:run_1500m) %>% as.matrix()
rownames(events) <- decathlon$athlete
decathlon_pca <- prcomp(events, scale. = TRUE)
decathlon_variance <- round(100 * summary(decathlon_pca)$importance[2, ], 1)
decathlon_loadings <- as_tibble(decathlon_pca$rotation[, 1:2], rownames = "event")
ggplot(decathlon_loadings) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = event)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", decathlon_variance[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", decathlon_variance[2], "%)"))
```

::: callout-note

### C. Guided: the whole root metabolome, without labels (16:00-16:35, pairs)

**C1. From long to wide.** One row per sample, one column per metabolite, log10 of the
concentration:

```r
root_wide <- metabolites %>%
  filter(organ == "root") %>%
  mutate(log_conc = log10(concentration)) %>%
  select(sample, genotype, water, heat, metabolite, log_conc) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = metabolite, values_from = log_conc)

root_matrix <- root_wide %>%
  select(-sample, -genotype, -water, -heat) %>%
  as.matrix()
rownames(root_matrix) <- root_wide$sample
```

`root_wide`: 31 rows, 38 columns (4 describing the sample + 34 metabolites).
`root_matrix`: 31 rows, 34 columns, numbers only.

**C2. The PCA.**

```r
root_pca <- prcomp(root_matrix, scale. = TRUE)

variance <- round(100 * summary(root_pca)$importance[2, ], 1)
variance
```

**C3. Where are the samples?** The PCA never saw `water` and `heat`: you only use them
now, to colour the points.

```r
root_scores <- as_tibble(root_pca$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  bind_cols(select(root_wide, sample, genotype, water, heat))

ggplot(root_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = water, shape = heat)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", variance[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", variance[2], "%)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-c3
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4

root_scores <- as_tibble(root_pca$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  bind_cols(select(root_wide, sample, genotype, water, heat))
ggplot(root_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = water, shape = heat)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", variance[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", variance[2], "%)"))
```

**C4. Which molecules drive the axes?**

```r
root_loadings <- as_tibble(root_pca$rotation[, 1:2], rownames = "metabolite") %>%
  arrange(PC1)

head(root_loadings, 5)   # most negative on PC1
tail(root_loadings, 5)   # most positive on PC1
```

**C5. The heatmap.** A small annotation table puts the conditions on top of the heatmap:

```r

  select(sample, water, heat) %>%
  column_to_rownames("sample")

pheatmap(t(root_matrix), scale = "row", annotation_col = annotation,
         show_colnames = FALSE, fontsize_row = 7)
```

```{r}
annotation <- root_wide %>% select(sample, water, heat) %>% column_to_rownames("sample")
pheatmap(t(root_matrix), scale = "row", annotation_col = annotation,
```

### D. Guided: with labels, then one test per molecule (16:35-17:10, pairs)

**D1. PLS-DA with the real labels.**

```r
root_plsda <- plsda(root_matrix, root_wide$water, ncomp = 2)

plotIndiv(root_plsda, ellipse = TRUE, legend = TRUE,
          title = "Root, PLS-DA with the real labels")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-d1
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Checkpoint D1: PLS-DA of the root, real labels."
root_plsda <- plsda(root_matrix, root_wide$water, ncomp = 2)
plotIndiv(root_plsda, ellipse = TRUE, legend = TRUE,
          title = "Root, PLS-DA with the real labels")
```

**D2. The trap.** Now give the PLS-DA labels that mean **nothing**: the same "drought"
and "watered" labels, mixed at random with `sample()`. Let it use 10 components, then ask
how well it classifies the samples it learned from:

```r
set.seed(1)
shuffled <- sample(root_wide$water)
root_plsda_shuffled <- plsda(root_matrix, shuffled, ncomp = 10)

predicted <- predict(root_plsda_shuffled, root_matrix)$class$max.dist[, 10]
mean(predicted == shuffled)
```

`set.seed(1)` makes the random draw the same for everyone, so that you can compare your
numbers.

**D3. Cross-validation.** The same two models, now judged on samples they did not learn
from:

```r
set.seed(1)
cv_shuffled <- perf(root_plsda_shuffled, validation = "Mfold", folds = 4, nrepeat = 10)
1 - cv_shuffled$error.rate$BER[10, "max.dist"]

set.seed(1)
cv_real <- perf(root_plsda, validation = "Mfold", folds = 4, nrepeat = 10)
1 - cv_real$error.rate$BER[2, "max.dist"]
```

::: callout-note
## Checkpoint

D2: the model learns the **random** labels almost perfectly (more than 90% correct on
its own data). D3: on samples it did not see, the same model is no better than tossing
a coin (around 50%), while the model with the real labels stays above 90%. Your exact
numbers can differ slightly with another version of mixOmics.
:::

**D4. One test per molecule.** The t-test of Session 4, run on each metabolite, then the
correction:

```r
root_tests <- metabolites %>%
  filter(organ == "root") %>%
  group_by(metabolite, panel) %>%
  summarise(log2_fold_change = log2(mean(concentration[water == "drought"]) /
                                    mean(concentration[water == "watered"])),
            p_value = t.test(log10(concentration) ~ water, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value,
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(p_adjusted = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"))
```

`log2_fold_change`: 1 means twice as high under drought, −1 half as high, 0 no change.

**D5. The volcano plot.**

```r
ggplot(root_tests, aes(x = log2_fold_change, y = -log10(p_adjusted), colour = panel)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_text_repel(data = slice_min(root_tests, p_adjusted, n = 10),
                  aes(label = metabolite), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-d5
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Checkpoint D5: volcano plot of the root, drought vs watered."
root_tests <- metabolites %>%
  filter(organ == "root") %>%
  group_by(metabolite, panel) %>%
  summarise(log2_fold_change = log2(mean(concentration[water == "drought"]) /
                                    mean(concentration[water == "watered"])),
            p_value = t.test(log10(concentration) ~ water, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value,
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(p_adjusted = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"))
ggplot(root_tests, aes(x = log2_fold_change, y = -log10(p_adjusted), colour = panel)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_text_repel(data = slice_min(root_tests, p_adjusted, n = 10),
                  aes(label = metabolite), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE)
```

The same plants seen by two methods. The workbook gives you the skeleton of the code: by
now, most of the `___` are the choices you made in C and D, so reuse your own code:

  stress dominates now?
- **F2**, the untargeted table: one row per plant, one column per feature (`F0001` to
  `F2500`), read directly in the wide format that metabolomics software produce. Some
  intensities are exactly 0, hence `log10(x + 1)`. Does the PCA tell the same story as the
  targeted list?
- **F3**, the PLS-DA trap again, with 2,500 variables and only 2 components: this time
  you can **see** it on the plot.
- **F4**, one test per feature: 2,500 tests, so the correction matters even more; then
  the names proposed for the significant features, in
  `soybean_exudates_annotation.csv`, and how much you can trust them; and the volcano

## Checkpoint

You are done when all of the following are true:

- you can explain why concentrations are log-transformed and scaled before a PCA;
- you turned a long table into a matrix with `pivot_wider()`;
- you can read a PCA: the share of variance, the scores and the loadings;
- you can read a heatmap with clustering, and say what its trees are computed from;
- you can explain why a PLS-DA that separates groups proves nothing until it is
  cross-validated, with the numbers of D2 and D3;
- you can read a volcano plot, and say why the p-values were adjusted;
- you can compare the leaf with the root, and say what is different;
- you can say what targeted and untargeted metabolomics each see, and why a putative
  name from an untargeted search is not an identification;
- you can say what the heatwave does to the exudates, and why it matters for the soil
  bacteria of Session 4.
